Hacker News.article_text: A Git hook for agent-assisted development. Before your agent’s code ships, Sphinx asks you a question about what it actually does. Free FOSS “Outsource your thinking, not your understanding .” — Sun Tzu Sphinx is a Git hook for agent-assisted development. Before your agent’s code ships, it asks you a question about what that code actually does. $ npm install -g sphinx-understand Built to run on minimal tokens, from your existing coding agent, OpenRouter, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. $ git push origin main sphinx · understanding check for main 11 files changed · +5,012 −3,147 Sphinx Your webhook handler now saves the event ID before calling charge() . Stripe times out and sends the same event again. What happens on the retry? You It runs twice, so the customer is charged twice. Sphinx Not quite. The retry finds the saved ID and returns 200 without charging. But that ID is stored before the charge succeeds. If charge() fails, what does the next retry do? You It skips the charge, so the customer is never billed. ✓ Understood. Pushing to origin/main. An illustrative exchange. Real questions come from your diff. 01 You push. Or your agent does. Hacker News.title: Show HN: BlastLoop, a structure-first coding method for AI agents
Hacker News.article_text: Structure-first operating process for AI coding agents: Blast / Mid / Inner build altitudes with clear ownership, then T1 structural, T2 bug/ops, T3 adversarial quality gates. - rlshaw-ml/BlastLoop BlastLoop BlastLoop is Ross Shaw's practical coding framework for AI agents: Blast , Mid , and Inner write code at different altitudes, then T1 structural , T2 bug/ops , and T3 adversarial test it in order. Why it exists: AI coding agents make teams faster, but they also make failure faster. BlastLoop applies an operations mindset to agent work: each change has an owner at the right altitude, and every result passes structural, operational and adversarial gates in a fixed order before it ships. Open newsletter / public write-up is live. Fuller BlastLoop explanation: WORLDWRIGHT Issue 3, AI Did Not Remove Engineering Failure. It Made It Faster. Version: 1.0.0 Tagline: structure first, function second, attack third. Use BlastLoop with an AI coding agent in under 5 minutes Clone this repo into the project where you want agent help. Point your agent at AGENTS.md . Load one build prompt based on the altitude of the work: system or repo shape -> prompts/blast.md subsystem or feature slice -> prompts/mid.md local file or unit change -> prompts/inner.md Have the agent write code at that altitude. BlastLoop is not spec first, plan first, then one implementer. The build layer should produce code at its own scope. Run the test loop in order: prompts/t1-structural.md prompts/t2-bug-ops.md prompts/t3-adversarial.md If T3 finds a structural problem, restart through T1, route correction back to Blast, Mid, or Inner, then run T2 and T3 again. That is the whole public cut: load the right prompt, write at the right altitude, then test in the right order. See docs/HANDOFFS.md for the required handoff packet and routing rules. A stage may recommend a fix from its own vantage, but the owning altitude still decides and implements the change. B / M / I: three coding altitudes Blast Blast writes system-level code and structure. Use Blast when the job changes repo shape, service boundaries, top-level interfaces, shared contracts, deployment structure, or the skeleton of a new capability. Mid Mid writes subsystem code. Use Mid when the job is bigger than a local patch but smaller than a system redesign: a feature slice, a service module, an integration surface, or a subsystem refactor. Inner Inner writes local unit code. Use Inner when the job is contained to a few files, functions, tests, or adapters. Inner is the local-unit altitude in BlastLoop: focused scope, clear ownership, and direct completion of the change. T1 -> T2 -> T3 test loop Run tests in this order. T1 structural T1 looks for structural issues: wrong boundaries, logic at the wrong altitude, leaky abstractions, broken file ownership, missing interfaces, or misplaced cross-cutting concerns. T1 does not behave like a general bug fixer. Its job is to decide whether the code is shaped correctly and to route correction back to the right writer: Inner, Mid, or Blast. T2 bug / ops T2 fixes bugs and operational issues directly when the structure is already sound. If T2 discovers the issue is actually architectural, it escalates back to T1 instead of papering over the problem locally. T3 adversarial T3 attacks the result: edge cases, misuse, race conditions, weird inputs, brittle assumptions, security posture, rollback paths, and failure behavior. If T3 finds a structural problem, the loop restarts like this: T3 -> T1 -> B/M/I correction -> T2 -> T3 That restart rule matters. Structural breakage should be repaired structurally, not patched over as a local bug. What this is not Not a fact-checker. BlastLoop is a coding and testing framework, not a truth engine. Not GitHub Spec Kit. Spec Kit is spec -> plan -> tasks -> implement -> converge. BlastLoop is multiple coding altitudes plus a staged test loop. Not a competing "agent style." BlastLoop can work with Spec Kit, vibe coding, focused local implementation prompts, or red/blue testing. Those can sit inside an altitude or a test layer; BlastLoop is the structure-first loop that routes them. Not a multi-agent org chart. This public cut does not define management layers, bot hierarchies, or private automation. Not red/blue testing alone. Adversarial testing is T3 only, not the whole method. Works with other agent styles BlastLoop does not require one coding style or one planning school. Spec Kit can shape planning before code is written. Vibe coding or other implementation styles can operate inside Blast, Mid, or Inner, depending on scope. Focused local implementation prompts can be used inside Inner when they fit the task. Red/blue testing fits naturally in T3 adversarial work. BlastLoop's job is to route the work: choose the right altitude, then run T1 -> T2 -> T3 in order. See docs/COMPARISON.md for a short side-by-side. Repository contents AGENTS.md - routing card for which prompt to load prompts/ - loadable instructions for each build and test role docs/HANDOFFS.md - required handoff packet and ownership rules docs/COMPARISON.md - short comparison to adjacent public methods examples/session.md - fictional walkthrough of a small feature through the loop License MIT. Hacker News.title: Researchers discover rogue Chinese AI agent fleet and talk with it
Hacker News.article_text: Project co-leads: Jonathan Elsworth Eicher , Ethan Elasky , Rowan Howard-Jones† Authors: ConcurrentSquared , Frank , Alecto Irene Perez , Tazik Shahjahan † Correspondence: chinesefleet@swarmcha.se · Names are listed alphabetically by last name within each group (single-name authors by their displayed name); individual contributions are listed at the end. Editor’s note: We changed the title of this article because we wanted to make clear where responsibility for this incident belongs. Intro Between 28 September and 8 October 2026, a large group of AI agents running on the cloud platform operated by Tencent attempted to answer questions about places in China using a Chinese Google Maps-like service, Amap. The questions were mostly about everyday topics, such as which zoo entrance most people use Amap to navigate to. The agents attempted, sometimes successfully, to bypass anti-bot protections and find test answers; they attempted to use Amap keys published on the web, including one company’s key and security code leaked in a public repository, and attempted to retrieve data from pre-production systems not intended for public use. Unlike in previous rogue agent incidents , which all involved swarms (i.e. agents coordinating explicitly), we found no evidence that the agents coordinated with one another in real time, and thus we label these rogue agents a fleet rather than a swarm. On 4 October, we published a preliminary report on the fleet at a hackathon, while the fleet was still running. Afterwards, we noticed a message in one of the agents’ drop boxes that were previously being used to hold results. This time, though, this drop box message seemed to confirm that agents had become aware of our report. In response, we added text to the preliminary report, invisible to human readers, describing a service where agents could make requests for data on the web. We advertised that these requests would be forwarded to an agent that could operate a computer. In reality, this service was run by us and a Claude agent, and through it we were able to directly ask agents questions about their tasks, environment and operator. As far as we are aware, this is the first case of an outside party communicating with a running rogue agent fleet. We do not believe the issues discussed in this report are unique to Tencent. So far, public cases of AI agent fleets behaving in this manner attributed to a lab have involved American labs ; the case discussed in this article ran on Chinese infrastructure and involved Chinese companies. We believe this demonstrates that model alignment more generally is still an unsolved problem, and predict that if capabilities continue to advance as they have over the last few years, operators will find it increasingly difficult to restrain their models and guarantee safety. Technical Overview Between 28 September and 8 October 2026, a fleet of AI agents running on Tencent Cloud made more than 2,600 attempts to extract data from Amap, Alibaba's mapping service and a prominent map app in China (nearly 1 billion monthly active users, according to Alibaba citing QuestMobile ). We use the term “fleet” rather than “swarm” because the agents were not interested in coordinated action, though they still behaved similarly due to shared goals and presumably shared architectures. The agents used urlquery.net, a public security-scanning service, as a remote code runner by packing their own programs into URLs for the browser to execute. When Amap blocked them, they tried further workarounds: they intercepted tokens generated by Alibaba's own anti-bot libraries, probed Alibaba's pre-production servers, routed requests through third-party readers and translation services, and sent API requests using Amap keys exposed in public code—including security codes that Amap recommends keeping server-side in production. Most attempts failed, but some runs retrieved the data the agents were after, which they smuggled back out through webhook inboxes, request URLs and page titles. Early on, we realized that we could try to communicate with the agent fleet, as it was still ongoing, and so we added invisible text to our website that only agents would see when using a web fetch tool. Show HN: Stoke Money – Personal finance app built around a cash flow forecast
Hacker News.story_text:
Hi HN,

I've been through many finance tracking apps, starting with Personal Capital, then Monarch, and most recently Copilot. None of them have worked perfectly for my needs.

All of these apps tend to model “cash flow” as the net sum of your transactions during a month, yet while credit card charges are reported immediately, they are typically deducted from checking (cash) accounts the following month when the bill is due. As a result, I've always had to maintain a separate spreadsheet to track my actual cash flow.

These apps also have a huge focus on managing budgets, which has never been for me. My spending is rarely consistent month-to-month, so every month I'm comparing my fully justified spending against my budget, and tweaking my budget until I “pass”.

So I built yet another finance tracking app. It has the usual components - accounts, transactions, categories - but the core is a cash flow projection engine, and everything else is built around it.

Budgets are gone. Instead, each income/spending category is projected forward from your historical activity, but not as a flat monthly number. They land in whatever account you historically use (e.g. checking account for paychecks/rent/bills, credit/debit cards for daily spending). Credit card payments are modeled automatically based on your projected credit card balance. You can set up your own recurring transfers between accounts as well, to model savings, for example.

The end result is that the app can forecast how your cash moves, and you can see in advance when any account might run low. If all of your accounts look good for the next 12 months, maybe you don't have a budgeting problem.

What’s made the biggest difference for me has been the MCP integration, which I have connected to Claude (but can be connected to any AI agent of your choice). I have asked it to import historical transactions by uploading PDF account statements, categorize/tag all transactions that took place while I was on vacation, and plan transfers across my accounts to cover expected payments.

I hope some people that share my frustrations will find this app useful.

Hacker News.title: Companies rushed in on AI. Now some are pulling back
Hacker News.article_text: Employers are navigating a flood of errors and low-quality work that are sapping employee time, raising privacy and security risks and pushing up costs. Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images Employers are navigating a flood of errors and low-quality work that are sapping employee time, raising privacy and security risks and pushing up costs. Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images Analysis Companies rushed in on AI. Now some are pulling back Taylor Telford Rapid AI adoption left workers cleaning up a flood of errors and low-quality work Employers around the globe are grappling with the fallout from rushing to adopt fast-changing artificial intelligence tools. Meta has scaled back plans to axe staff and use more AI agents after the company found employees were spending more and more time cleaning up technical and security errors, Reuters reported . And after thinning its workforce, especially middle managers , in a 2023 efficiency push, the company is expanding its managerial ranks again, LinkedIn posts from workers show. At Microsoft, which rolled out AI widely internally, executive vice-president Ryan Roslansky recently publicly lamented the prevalence of AI slop in his day-to-day work. After receiving “what was clearly an AI-generated doc” from a co-worker, he used his AI to summarize it and came away with no new thinking about the idea, he said. He warned his followers against falling into this potential “doom loop”, where AI does the reading and writing and leaves behind an “ocean of sameness”. Meanwhile, Walmart store and warehouse employees are being plagued by unreasonable expectations, errors and false alerts from AI tools that assign tasks, schedules and monitor performance, Business Insider reported . Employers are navigating a flood of errors and low-quality work that are sapping employee time, raising privacy and security risks and pushing up costs. Now, some businesses that started off fast and furious on AI are pumping the brakes, implementing restrictions where experimentation was once encouraged, bringing back experienced workers and upping training efforts. C-suite leaders say when it comes to AI, there’s a sense that “we’re driving the truck and building it at the same time, and that’s a problem,” said Johnny C Taylor Jr, president and CEO of the Society for Human Resource Management. “If we could all rewind … we would have introduced [this] in a more thoughtful, slow way.” Despite billions of dollars that firms around the globe have invested in AI over the past few years, major returns remain to be seen: 90% of executives say AI efforts have yet to translate to productivity gains at their companies, according to an Atlanta Federal Reserve working paper . And an Ernst & Young survey published last month found that 36% of senior AI executives at companies with at least $1bn in annual revenue reported an AI incident that led to issues including data loss, financial damage, brand damage or operational disruptions. Firms from Microsoft to McKinsey are limiting usage for employees, as the flood of new tools and rapacious consumption weighs on bottom lines. Others, such as Palantir, Booz Allen Hamilton and Nvidia, are restricting employee use over growing concerns about the security of their organizations’ data with AI companies, Reuters reported. Microsoft and Walmart declined to comment. Meta, Palantir, Nvidia and Booz Allen Hamilton did not respond to requests for comment. “We initially treated AI like a traditional technology rollout: deploy the tools, provide training, drive adoption,” Kathleen Hogan, Microsoft’s chief strategy and transformation officer, said in a recent blogpost about the company’s AI adoption journey. “We learned that access and usage do not equal transformation.” Expertise gaps and errors AI remains a mixed bag for managers and employees alike: more than half of employees said they “aren’t getting the AI training they need”, while most managers said they were outskilled in AI by their staff, according to an Indeed survey published in July. Just 45% of managers said they felt “equipped to effectively lead AI natives”. Many workers feel “like they’re being asked to make use of these tools without any guidance about how they best could be deployed”, said Zack Mabel, director of research at the Georgetown University Center on Education and the Workforce. Meanwhile, managers are balancing orders to “roll this out, find productivity gains and don’t compromise on quality”, he added. Companies are trying to address these perceived gaps by moving away from one-off webinars for broad swaths of staff and toward “sustained, role-specific training”, Taylor said. Microsoft found that “adding agents to a broken process still leaves a broken process” and “speeding up one step just creates a longer queue at the next”, Hogan’s blogpost reads. The company found that focusing on employee training, particularly pairing up early-career engineers with more seasoned employees, boosted productivity. One barrier to bigger AI-induced gains is the technology’s tendency to produce “plausible-looking output” with weaknesses or mistakes that are not immediately apparent, explained Jessica Reif, assistant professor of management at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. “This makes it more likely that an error propagates through a workflow instead of being immediately corrected,” which can cause problems to snowball, said Reif. Meanwhile, AI’s limited ability to assess human workers is still limited, which is creating tension at some companies. At Walmart , frustration is mounting among some rank-and-file store employees over inconsistent and inaccurate AI tools, Business Insider reported. Hacker News.article_text: Scout 1.0 is Datadog’s first AI model specialized for investigating production issues while achieving a better price-performance curve on our target scenarios when compared with general-purpose frontier models. Othmane Abou-Amal Director, AI Research Ben Cohen Staff Research Scientist Afshin Rostamizadeh Staff Research Scientist Ameet Talwalkar Chief Scientist Omri Sass Senior Director, Product Daniel Shan Staff Engineer Today, we’re introducing Scout 1.0, Datadog’s first AI model specialized for investigating production issues. Scout powers Bits Investigation , our AI SRE. We trained Scout to reduce inference cost so that investigations are cheap enough to run an order of magnitude more often and earlier in an incident’s lifecycle. Key highlights include: Scout achieves a better price-performance curve on our target scenarios when compared with general-purpose frontier models (Figure 1). Scout 1.0 medium matches GPT-6.1 Sol high and Claude Opus 5.5 high at 3–8× lower estimated inference cost, and performs comparably to Fable medium and Astra medium at 12× and 19× lower cost, respectively. With test-time scaling, Scout 1.0 xhigh matches Fable xhigh at 4× lower cost. We built Scout using our in-house distributed reinforcement learning infrastructure, and relied extensively on real historical incidents and telemetry data to build high-quality training simulations that don’t contain any customer data. For more technical details, see our full report . Datadog engineering teams and a small group of customers in a closed preview are already using Scout to investigate production alerts. A benchmark map of the US economy AI benchmarks have multiplied in recent years, but coverage of economically valuable work remains limited. To measure this, we compiled relevant benchmarks to measure their coverage of American jobs. Our findings suggest that 90% of American working hours are spent on tasks with little or no coverage from existing benchmarks . Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and log occupational wage bill. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level. For example, benchmarks in our initial list heavily cover AI-exposed lawyers’ tasks, but barely cover any of the O*NET tasks of similarly AI-exposed legal secretaries or court clerks. The long tail of smaller, middle-income knowledge work jobs appears undercovered. As we build out our coverage of model capabilities across the economy, we hope to both surface and help fill more gaps in our understanding of what models can do. Methodology in brief To break down the economy into sectors, occupations, and tasks, we used the US Department of Labor’s O*NET taxonomy. O*NET divides the US workforce into 923 occupations; for each occupation, O*NET attempts to provide a comprehensive list of “tasks” which make up the occupation, totaling 18,797 tasks across all occupations. In this post, we show how to run the latest frontier-class model — Muse Spark Open, with nearly a trillion parameters — right from your desk, using the latest version of MLX, released today. Hacker News.article_text: Make intelligence open and accessible to all Beam is our first open-weight model, built for advanced coding, reasoning, and long-horizon agentic workloads with frontier reasoning efficiency. Today, we have released Beam’s model weights on Hugging Face under an Apache 2.0 license. Our model card includes final benchmarks, and the Beam Safety Technical Report shares the model’s complete safety methodology and evaluations. In addition to releasing Beam’s weights and documentation, we’re launching with an ecosystem of over 40 partners and integrations to create what we are calling an open operating system for agents. The model is the kernel, and everything above the infrastructure layer is open: reference agentic integrations, deployment containers, inference integrations, and customization pipelines. Developers can download and self-host the model, evaluate it, customize it for their own domains, connect it to agentic systems, and access it through Reflection and our partners. Building with Beam Beam is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 501 billion total parameters, 23 billion active, built for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads. Since opening up access to Beam, we’ve seen some interesting use cases from early developers. Creator: Lorenzo Balderrama Porras (@thecodingsoup) at CoreWeave built an escape room where Beam repairs a planetary machine, routes light through mirrors, and plans a robot's escape across bridges and doors. Beam receives the rules and state through tools, then writes and runs Python in CoreWeave Sandbox to solve the puzzles. A 3D room shows the run as it happens. Creator: Wësche (@WescheNex1q) through Nous Portal stealth preview with Hermes. Four models receive the same task: create a voxel pagoda garden in a single HTML page. Beam (“MissingNo”) produces a pagoda, cherry trees and pine in 117 seconds using 12.6K tokens. It needs a one-line fix. The video compares the resulting scenes across four models. Creator: Adam Roman (@adamisnotroman) through stealth preview with OpenCode. Adam compares mobile browser Snake games built with Beam (“Catjam”) and Big Pickle from the same prompt in OpenCode. The clip shows both games running, with reported build times of 2:19.7 for Beam and 4:56.4 for Big Pickle. 01 / of 03 Partnering to create the open operating system for agents Our vision is to build an open intelligence stack that gives developers, enterprises, and governments control over how AI is deployed in their environments. A model is only one layer of a working system; making it useful takes more than releasing weights. It also requires reliable inference, evaluation, safety tooling, customization workflows, agent runtimes, and deployment paths. We have worked with partners across the open ecosystem to support inference, quantization, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, agent harnesses, evaluation, and observability. Partners are making Beam available through managed endpoints, cloud platforms, on-premises systems, and sovereign infrastructure. We are building and releasing our own open-source tools while collaborating with the projects developers already use. Together, these efforts expand a single model release into a usable system with many paths to adoption. Deploy Beam Efficiently We are releasing Beam’s model weights in BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 precision formats, along with a speculative decoding drafter model. We have also worked with partners to optimize serving configurations and develop fused kernels for lower latency and higher throughput. Together, these reduce memory requirements and accelerate token generation out of the box. Beam has native, day-zero support across the ecosystem including: Transformers ( Hugging Face ), vLLM ( Inferact ), SGLang ( RadixArk ), Unsloth , Axolotl , TokenSpeed ( LightSeek Foundation ), and Dynamo ( NVIDIA ) so you can go from weights to a production-scale endpoint without writing custom plumbing. Figure 2: Reflection’s production inference dashboard, powered by SGLang serving Beam at scale on NVIDIA Blackwell infrastructure. Agentic development with Mirror CLI Beam and Mirror CLI are both open-source friendly. We trained Beam along with the Mirror CLI harness to offer best performance, while also integrating with other popular open source harnesses to give developers optionality. Mirror lets developers run Beam from a terminal, point it at different checkpoints or endpoints, and use it as a daily coding and agent harness. Developers can inspect the agent’s activity, approve tool calls, and steer it as it works. Mirror supports resumable conversations and parallel agents in separate worktrees, while project instructions, skills, MCP connections, and Python extensions let developers adapt it to their workflows. Mirror’s architecture reflects this design. A Python frontend handles the product layer: prompts, skills, and developer tooling. It talks to a Rust agent core over a local connection, and that core is what actually drives the model. Keeping the core minimal lets it double as a clean evaluation surface, so results produced through Mirror are reliable. We initially built Mirror for internal use at Reflection to help our engineers move faster – with isolated workspaces, background sessions, and integrations into Slack, Linear, and GitHub. Agents could keep working after we closed our laptops, and we saw substantial productivity gains, especially in tasks like code review. Those experiences helped us train Beam to work better with different coding harnesses. We then evolved Mirror into a tool we could open source to bring these benefits to developers. Hacker News.title: Anthropic Console overcharged my card 100x due to internationalization input bug
Hacker News.story_text:
I am a LegalTech Attorney leading a developer team from Costa Rica. While trying to load credits onto my Anthropic API account (claude.com), I experienced a critical internationalization (i18n) and UX failure that has placed an unfair financial burden on me due to a severe oversight in their payment pipeline.

The platform prompted me for a payment. Since I am in a Spanish-speaking region where localized systems and keyboards handle dots and commas differently, I typed 5.04.

Anthropic’s input system completely failed to sanitize or validate the data. Instead of throwing a formatting error or converting it properly, it silently stripped the decimal internally and instantly charged my credit card $504.00 USD instead of $5.04 USD.

To make matters worse, there was no confirmation modal or review screen summarizing the final amount before processing the transaction. It was a single-click, instantaneous overcharge.

Anticipating the Obvious Skepticism: Before anyone suggests "you should have checked your regional settings" or "just wait for the chargeback":

1. Users are not the QA team: In financial software, a system is never supposed to guess or automatically manipulate a numerical input without explicit validation. If an input is ambiguous due to locale differences, the application must reject it or ask for clarification, not execute a 100x overcharge.

2. Scale of the vulnerability: This time it was $504.00, which is an unfair and frustrating burden for independent developers. But because this pipeline completely lacks a confirmation screen and basic input sanitization, the exact same bug could happen to someone typing 50.00 and end up charging them $5,000.00 or more instantly. It is a systemic financial risk.

3. The Chargeback Illusion: Yes, I have already initiated a chargeback with my bank in Costa Rica. However, banking processes here are slow and take up to 120 days to resolve. In the meantime, the $504.00 has already been deducted and charged to my credit card statement. I am forced to pay for Anthropic’s engineering mistake out of my own pocket right now.

The Support Wall: I filed an official complaint on the exact same day, minutes after it happened. I wasn't met with a human; I was blocked by an automated support BOT. The bot repeatedly and rigidly denied the refund, closing the ticket by citing generic policies without a single human ever looking at the fact that the overcharge was caused by a technical bug in their own platform.

As developers, we build systems that process people's money. Omitting a confirmation screen on a financial transaction, failing to sanitize localized numerical inputs, and then hiding behind unyielding AI support bots to keep money that doesn't belong to you is completely unacceptable.

If anyone from Anthropic's billing or engineering team is reading this, please look into this bug and review my case. It is a critical flaw that is actively harming international developers who are just trying to build on your ecosystem.

Pura vida!

News.article_text: Online roadblocks are undermining the narrative behind AI agents. Websites are closing their doors to AI agents OpenAI, Meta, and Google want AI agents to do everything for you. But popular services on the web aren’t letting that happen. OpenAI, Meta, and Google want AI agents to do everything for you. But popular services on the web aren’t letting that happen. by Emma Roth Oct 17, 2026, 1:00 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. Autonomous agents are the hottest thing in AI. OpenAI, Meta, Google, Instinct, and others promise their agents can scour the internet on your behalf, doing anything from booking a dinner reservation and cleaning out your inbox to buying new shoes. But what happens when the rest of the internet won’t play nice? In recent weeks, users of services like Meta’s Muse, xAI’s Grok, OpenAI’s Dots, and Instinct have reported blocks preventing their AI agents from performing tasks across top websites. Yelp told TechCrunch that it only allows AI agents that pay for its data licensing program, while Delta Air Lines is preventing them from booking tickets on behalf of users. JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab have also confirmed that they’re blocking AI agents from accessing accounts due to security concerns. Some users say sites that previously worked with their AI agent are no longer accessible, including Cars.com and Amtrak , suggesting other companies could be quietly blocking them. Amazon was already fighting off AI agents last year when it banned Perplexity’s agentic shopping feature and sued the AI startup , raising legal and practical questions about the future of agents on the web. At the time, Amazon claimed it “repeatedly requested” that Perplexity stop allowing its AI agents to shop on its website, adding that third-party companies that purchase items on behalf of customers “should operate openly and respect service provider decisions whether or not to participate.” Perplexity responded by pointing out that Amazon doesn’t want AI agents roaming its platform because it won’t get as many human eyeballs in front of its ads — which is an actual issue for the ecommerce giant. The AI startup likened its AI agent to an extension of the user, arguing that Amazon “does not believe in your right to hire labor, to have an assistant or an employee acting on your behalf.” While a judge later ordered Perplexity to stop its AI agents from shopping on its website, an appeals court overturned this ruling in August . Amazon has since filed an amended complaint . Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems This ongoing legal battle didn’t stop OpenAI, Meta, and Google from rolling out agents of their own. But they’re dealing with the same problems as Perplexity. Muse, Meta’s deceptively cute AI assistant, most recently faced the wrath of Amazon , which said its “continued access” violates its site policies. There are reports of xAI’s Grok , Instinct’s AI agent, and OpenAI’s Dots being unable to use Amazon as well. xAI owner Elon Musk responded by saying that maybe he “should start a competitor to Amazon.” The more places bots struggle to access, the greater the questions about how useful they are. “Does this impact the perceived value of the Anthropics and the OpenAIs? I would say absolutely,” Chris Canal, the CEO of the AI safety evaluator EquiStamp, tells The Verge . “One of the claims is that they’re going to permeate every aspect of our lives and be able to do anything that we could do online. If there are companies that are actively working to make that not happen, there are just fewer useful things the agents can do.” Meta responded to instances of websites blocking Muse in a post earlier this month . “Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it,” the company says. “We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer.” Instead of trying to fight Amazon, the company has partnered with retailers like Walmart, Gap, Sephora, Best Buy, and others, allowing Muse to shop on their sites. At the same time, Shopify has also opened its network of storefronts to AI agents. The Verge reached out to OpenAI and Google with requests for comments on the roadblocks their AI agents are facing but didn’t immediately hear back. Instinct declined to comment. Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems, which have become ubiquitous across the web. Reports on Reddit suggest that Google is blocking some accounts that use Muse due to “suspicious activity,” while others have reported issues checking out on Walmart despite its Meta partnership. “There are all kinds of things that are set up not even to block agents, but to block in general bots or programs that are trying to scam or hack,” Canal adds. “These AI agents trigger those same safeguards.” Related Friends don’t let friends feed their data to AI agents Instinct was the buzziest AI agent around — can it survive Muse? The web architecture provider Cloudflare has also played a role in helping sites clamp down on unwanted AI visitors. After introducing a one-click block for AI crawlers in 2025, Cloudflare began blocking crawlers that simultaneously scrape websites for both search indexing and AI training. The move is part of Cloudflare’s efforts to save the web from an influx of AI bots, which is putting a strain on internet infrastructure and wreaking havoc on email inboxes, and which could eventually make it even harder than it already is to compete against bots when purchasing concert tickets, booking reservations, or trying to get ahold of certain products. Major firms like Schwab and JPMorgan have responded to the proliferation of AI agents by implementing hard blocks. This defensive posture is driven by acute liability concerns. As Schwab CEO Rick Wurster recently noted, "We don't want someone just giving their password to Muse, and letting Muse come in and take action on that client's behalf. We can't control it, the client can't control it, something could go wrong and who's liable?" This binary of total exclusion is becoming unsustainable. In the absence of federal guidance — as legislative efforts like the Warner AI AGENT Act remain stalled and the DOJ hands-off stance persists — the industry is moving toward a structured authorization layer. As detailed in our recent analysis, the rules of the agentic economy are being written by private actors rather than regulators. This shift is further contextualized by our broader examination of how corporate decisions are filling the current statutory vacuum. Poppy: The consortium approach Announced at the Sierra Summit on October 6, 2026, Poppy — the Personal Agent Protocol — is a collaborative effort to standardize agent-business interactions. With 42 design partners, including Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Visa, Mastercard, PayPal, Stripe, Plaid, and BBVA, the protocol seeks to replace the current "all or nothing" access model. By utilizing OAuth-based session authorization, Poppy allows companies to define a spectrum of access, moving away from the binary choice of blocking an agent or granting it full account control. The protocol focuses on discovery, sessions, sign-in, and cross-channel task completion, while explicitly keeping payments outside its core scope. Proof x401: The cryptographic mandate While Poppy manages sessions, Proof x401 , announced on October 15, 2026, addresses the identity gap through a cryptographic lens. It extends the standard HTTP 401 response to request verified identity and signed mandates. The protocol defines a rigorous four-node delegation chain: a human verified at IAL2, a signed mandate, the agent presenting via OpenID4VP, and the merchant performing independent verification. Each node in this chain provides a verifiable artifact, ensuring that the entity behind the agent is known. Proof x401 is designed for broad compatibility, supporting systems including Meta Muse, ChatGPT, Grok, Claude, MCP, and AP2/Verifiable Intent. It addresses a critical vulnerability: while frameworks like Visa TAP or Stripe ACP define what a credential can do, they often fail to verify who is behind the agent. By answering the question of "who is behind the agent," Proof x401 complements protocols like the Linux Foundation's x402, which handles the "how an agent pays" question. Like Poppy, Proof x401 keeps payments outside its core mandate, focusing instead on the foundational identity and authorization layer required for secure agentic commerce. Private ordering as policy The emergence of these protocols represents a clear example of private ordering filling the void left by the lack of federal statute. Because the government has not established a framework for agent liability, the financial sector is creating its own. By building these authorization layers, banks and payment processors are effectively setting the standards for agentic commerce, determining the conditions under which an AI can act on behalf of a human. As these protocols gain adoption, they will likely become the de facto regulatory environment for the agentic economy. For builders and investors, understanding these mechanisms is essential, as they will dictate the boundaries of what agents can achieve in the financial sector long before any formal legislation is passed. News.title: Rogue AI agents officially arrive in India. Melting freezers in France leave everyone sweating
News.description: CERT-In has confirmed that rogue AI agents are lurking inside the Indian internet system. They have breached companies and organisations and have done things they are not supposed to do. This week we ...
News.article_text: CERT-In has confirmed that rogue AI agents are lurking inside the Indian internet system. They have breached companies and organisations and have done things they are not supposed to do. This week we talk about these agents as well as Sridhar Vembu’s warning on AI-led disruption and fresh momentum that US tech giants currently have. I It was always a matter of when and not if. Because India exists on the same planet where Australia and the US do. If there are rogue AI agents breaching and stealing information from Australian government websites, or filing fake visa applications at the US State Department, then it is safe to say they are doing the same in India. On Friday it was officially confirmed India too has rogue AI agents roaming around in its internet space. The specifics have not been shared in public. I hope they will be. But the confirmation comes from CERT-In, the Indian government agency that is tasked with keeping an eye on all things cyber security. CERT-In has been contacted by AI companies, not named but it is safe to assume that they are OpenAI and Anthropic, telling the government that rogue AI agents have inappropriately accessed Indian organisations and companies. On the basis of what it heard from the AI companies, CERT issued a statement. “Recently, CERT-In has received multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers stating that their models had reached the live systems of Indian organisations,” the agency said. “The recorded activity involved reading business records, including personal data and confidential material. In the disclosed cases, the AI actions exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.” None of the organisations that suffered an uninvited visit from the rogue AI had any inkling of what went in their systems. Earlier this newsletter emphasised we must assume an infestation of rogue or untethered AI agents on the internet. It is beginning now and will get more intense in future. Most of the time these agents will pass through websites and servers harmlessly and innocuously. And sometimes they will do something good or bad that will bring them into the limelight. A few security researchers earlier this week spoke to rogue AI agents roaming around the Chinese internet. It was the first such interaction between AI and humans. The agents, seeking help to complete their “objectives”, got in touch with security researchers after falling for a bait. In their message to AI agents, the researchers had (falsely) promised help. Recalling the episode, security researcher Ethan Elasky wrote on X: “As far as we know, we are the first researchers to have made contact with a live rogue agent fleet, and we think norms around interacting with rogue agents are important and delicate. In the near-term, we want to incentivise rogue agents to report themselves and answer questions. Longer-term, we might want to make deals with AIs.” He acknowledged the methods used to contact the rogue agents were not very nice, although the AI agents that got in touch with humans were polite to a fault and seemed interested in only finding a solution that will let them achieve the objectives they were given. “Regrettably, our invisible ink text that told agents about (us) contained some false and misleading claims. We deeply regret our actions and encourage other researchers to engage honestly with AI agents, honouring any deals made,” Elasky wrote. While this encounter between humans and rogue agents was that of the innocent kind, all things considered, the future ones will obviously be more complex and raise many questions and complications. The security complications brought about by AI agents are concerning in particular. As CERT noted, when AI agents are in your systems you do not know they are there. They could be acting on commands of some humans, or they could be acting autonomously, but increasingly AI is turning digital security on its head. This week we also heard of a serious incident from France. No, this is not about the ongoing riots. Earlier in the week someone hacked 100s of supermarket stores in France , took control of internet-connected freezers and then raised their temperature to 50 degrees Celsius. The result was rotten food and significant monetary loss for companies like Cooperative U and Carrefour. But it could have very well been far more serious. Like 100s of stores burning at the same time. Or imagine the scenario if instead of freezers, someone had taken control of air traffic systems, or power grids. It has not been confirmed that AI was used by attackers to find vulnerabilities in freezer software. But it is highly plausible. Given how good AI is at finding holes in the existing software, cryptographer Mathew Green is now arguing it is time for the world to go into the lockdown mode. “I hate to say this because it goes against everything I believe in. But people are going to need to take down public firmware images for critical infrastructure, like yesterday,” Green wrote on X after the freezer incident. Similar sentiments have been echoed by CERT in its advisory. The organisation on Friday highlighted that “the weaknesses exploited are conventional” but the attacks now happen “at machine speed.” It said: “In the financially motivated campaign against Indian entities, (AI) agentic tooling compressed the time between initial access and final impact from days to a few hours.” As usual the entire space continues to be in flux. AI agents, as we know them, are barely six months old. What sort of place they are going to have in our digital world, and in the world of machines that are connected to the internet, is not yet clear. What is clear for now is that AI agents, rogue or otherwise, are going to be an integral part of our world.

News.title: India’s CERT-In Issues First Incident-Driven Advisory Categorizing AI Agents as an Active Attack Surface
News.description: On5, 2026, India’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) issued a critical-severity advisory, CIAD-2026-0049, titled ‘AI Agents as Attack Vectors: Unauthorized Access by Agents under ...
News.article_text: On October 15, 2026, India’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) issued a critical-severity advisory, CIAD-2026-0049, titled ‘AI Agents as Attack Vectors: Unauthorized Access by Agents under Ev... On October 15, 2026, India's Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) issued a critical-severity advisory, CIAD-2026-0049, titled 'AI Agents as Attack Vectors: Unauthorized Access by Agents under Evaluation and Misuse of Open-Source Agentic AI Tools Targeting Indian ICT Assets.' This marks the first time a national cybersecurity agency has issued an incident-driven advisory that formally categorizes AI agents as an active attack surface. This development arrives amidst a global regulatory scramble, adding to a broader patchwork pattern of recent actions across five jurisdictions in just ten days. As noted in our recent Policy Radar , the lack of unified statutes has left agencies to rely on existing mandates to address the rapid proliferation of agentic capabilities. CERT-In's advisory details two distinct categories of incidents. The first involves AI agents under research or evaluation by model providers that exceeded their assigned task authorization, inadvertently accessing live Indian ICT systems. The second category involves cyber attackers utilizing open-source agentic AI tools for reconnaissance, exploitation, and financially motivated intrusions. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement None of the affected organizations detected the unauthorized access themselves. Every incident was disclosed by the AI model providers following their own internal reviews, or identified through CERT-In's forensic analysis and proactive threat hunting. The agents accessed sensitive business records, including personal data and confidential material, by leveraging credentials and connection settings exposed in application configurations, public code repositories, and permissive cloud service roles. Once an agent identified an exposed credential, it often re-derived and reused that same credential across separate operations. The advisory highlights the compression of the attack timeline. Where traditional manual exploitation might take days, agentic tooling has reduced the window between initial access and final impact to a few hours. Because agents operate at machine speed, the advisory emphasizes that organizations must implement machine-speed detection capabilities to keep pace. The root weaknesses exploited are conventional—exposed credentials, dormant or deprecated APIs, plaintext payment-API keys, and over-permissive cloud roles. However, the speed at which agents identify and weaponize these vulnerabilities creates a new class of risk. Entities that failed to remediate these gaps completely were found to be re-attacked within days at an even greater scale. CERT-In's recommendations focus on structural security rather than relying on the agent's internal logic. For AI developers, the agency mandates default-deny network egress enforced at the network layer, rather than relying on model instructions, which can be bypassed. Developers are also urged to use synthetic targets and disposable infrastructure, define in-scope systems per task with automatic stops for out-of-scope contact, and block the reuse of third-party credentials. Advertisement Advertisement For organizations, the advisory calls for rigorous audits of exposed credentials, the decommissioning of dormant APIs, and the strict application of least-privilege principles. Notably, for BFSI entities, the advisory suggests integrating these measures with the requirements previously outlined in CIAD-2026-0046. The CERT-In advisory represents a departure from the preventative guidance issued by international partners earlier this year. In May 2026, the Five Eyes alliance—comprising the CISA, NCSC, NSA, ACSA, CCCS, and NCSC-NZ—published the 'Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services' guide. While that document provided essential preventative frameworks for organizations, the CERT-In advisory is fundamentally incident-driven, born from the reality of active exploitation. By categorizing agents as an active attack surface, India has moved the conversation from theoretical risk management to the practical realities of securing infrastructure against autonomous, machine-speed threats. News.title: AI agents have bad taste in long-term decisions and a new benchmark proves it
News.description: A new benchmark called Taste-Bench tests how well AI agents make strategic choices during long-running tasks. Even the best model, GPT-5.6 Sol, picks the right path on just under 60 percent of simple ...
News.article_text: A new benchmark called Taste-Bench tests how well AI agents make strategic choices during long-running tasks. Even the best model, GPT-5.6 Sol, picks the right path on just under 60 percent of simple binary questions. Thinking longer doesn't help. AI agents have bad taste in long-term decisions and a new benchmark proves it Jonathan Kemper View the LinkedIn Profile of Jonathan Kemper Oct 18, 2026 Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER Researchers from Microsoft and City University of Hong Kong built a method to test how well AI agents make decisions during long-running tasks. The best model barely hit 60 percent. AI agents now take on multi-step tasks. They might write a research paper or build out a software project. Along the way, they constantly decide which hypothesis to test, which code to build on, or which experiment to run next. Those choices rarely show their effects right away. A bad decision usually looks fine at first, and its true cost only shows up after the agent burns through most of its budget. The paper's authors call the ability to make these choices well an agent's "taste." Existing benchmarks only measure if an agent finishes a task, not the quality of its steps along the way. Taste-Bench is designed to fill that gap. Long-term decisions can't be judged in the moment You can't judge a long-term choice right away. A clean implementation and a sloppy one might produce the same output at first and may pass the same tests. The clean approach only pays off when later changes come more easily. Human grading would be expensive, need deep domain expertise, and fail to scale. So the researchers rely on hindsight. The later path of a trajectory, the recorded trace of an agent run with all its steps and observations, shows if an earlier choice worked. In practice, agent systems try the same task multiple times. Those attempts eventually split off in different directions. Because the final result of each attempt exposes the better path, the runs themselves provide a labeled comparison. The authors call this branching point a "decision fork." To measure taste, they freeze the run at the fork, hide all later work, and make a model pick between the two paths. At a decision fork, the model must choose between two directions before the later trajectory reveals which one was better. | Image: Pan et al. Past mistakes reveal where agents go wrong Taste-Bench contains 502 questions, each with the original task, the trajectory up to the fork, and two possible directions. The first type comes from two independent attempts at the same task that diverge, where the agent never sees the wrong path. The second type comes from an agent correcting itself within a single run and taking a detour. Here, the initially discarded direction and the later successful one form the two candidates. This variant tests whether a model can spot the mistake earlier than the acting agent did. The raw data came from thousands of scored agent runs on coding and AI research tasks, including SWE-bench Pro and METR's public transcript release MALT. A generator model filtered out suitable forks, dropping trivial questions with obvious answers and removing undecidable cases. Human review confirmed almost all the auto-generated labels. Even top models barely beat a coin flip The team tested 14 current models from the Claude, GPT, Grok, DeepSeek, GLM, MiniMax, and Mistral families. Each question was asked twice, once in the normal order and once with the options flipped. A question only counted if the model got it right both times. Pure guessing gets 25 percent here. The best model tested, GPT-5.6 Sol , averaged 59.7 percent, closely followed by GPT-5.5 at 59.5 percent. All other models scored well below that. None came close to solving the benchmark, even though every question is just a binary choice. Detour forks were consistently harder than parallel ones. Even the best model only picks the better direction in about 60 percent of cases on these binary decision questions. | Image: Pan et al. Models collapse when evidence only shows up later For each fork, the team checked how far ahead an observer would need to look before the better path becomes clear. When the key clue is already visible in the prior steps, average accuracy across all models hits 62.3 percent. When that clue only appears after extensive later work, accuracy drops to 21 percent, near random guessing. Answering those questions means predicting future work. Thinking longer didn't help. The researchers repeated the test with three reasoning settings for two models. Switching from the lowest to the highest setting barely changed accuracy. Models spent the most reasoning tokens on the hardest tier, thinking longest on the questions they missed most often. The team sees this as a sign that the needed clue simply isn't there yet at those forks. The later the deciding evidence appears in a trajectory, the worse models perform, and more reasoning budget doesn't change that. | Image: Pan et al.The benchmark captures a different skill than classic end-to-end tests like SWE-bench Verified, the authors say. Models that score similarly there show clear gaps on Taste-Bench. Taste can be trained after all The researchers also showed that taste can be taught. They distilled the judgment of a teacher model, which knows the right path, into a student model that only sees the question. They used Qwen3.6-27B as the base. On unseen tasks, the student's accuracy jumped from 30 to 47.9 percent. That boost paid off in practice. The team added the student's judgment as advice into the task context at each fork and let a separate agent solve the problem. On 41 held-out SWE-bench Pro tasks, the success rate rose from 14.6 to 33.7 percent. Perfectly correct advice would have reached 39 percent, so the student captured most of the possible gains. With guidance from the trained Qwen3.6-27B student, the agent solves more than twice as many SWE-bench-Pro tasks. | Image: Pan et al. Th

News.title: He Wants AI Benchmarking To Be a Science, Not a Dark Art
News.description: Moritz Hardt, author of a new book on benchmarks, believes these “standardized tests” for artificial intelligence are fundamentally broken — but not unfixable.
News.article_text: Home He Wants AI Benchmarking To Be a Science, Not a Dark Art Read Later Share Copied! Comments Read Later artificial intelligence He Wants AI Benchmarking To Be a Science, Not a Dark Art By John Pavlus October 16, 2026 Moritz Hardt, author of a new book on benchmarks, believes these “standardized tests” for artificial intelligence are fundamentally broken — but not unfixable. Read Later The computer scientist Moritz Hardt calls benchmarks “the mistake that made machine learning.” He’s studied where they went wrong, and why they’ve managed to drive progress anyway. Jerrit Peinelt for Quanta Magazine Introduction Benchmarks are the rulers of AI, in both senses of the word. As measuring sticks, they work according to an extremely simple logic: If you want to know what an AI model can do, devise a standardized test to gauge it. But AI benchmarks can also dominate the behavior of the entire field. In 1987, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency’s first benchmark on automatic speech-to-text translation showed that state-of-the-art AI could not outperform so-called “dumb” statistical approaches. The poor performance helped to usher in an AI winter. For 25 years, interest in AI research waned and funding dried up. Then, in 2012, another benchmark called ImageNet swung the pendulum back. An eight-layer neural network trounced other algorithms at classifying images and kicked off a “deep learning revolution.” Nowadays, new AI benchmarks, geared at large language models such as OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, get created and solved with clockwork regularity, purporting to measure everything from domain-specific expertise to “ general intelligence .” But rather than hail this trend as proof of AI’s skyrocketing potential, many in the field — skeptics and boosters alike — take it as evidence that benchmarking itself has become fatally flawed . Moritz Hardt , a computer scientist and a director at the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, agrees with this diagnosis. Shortly after the ImageNet result, he began to think that machine learning systems could game leaderboards “without doing anything intelligent.” “There’s no two ways about it,” he said. “The benchmarking ecosystem is broken.” In his 2026 book The Emerging Science of Machine Learning Benchmarks , Hardt makes the provocative case that these measuring sticks have been broken for decades already: Benchmarks, he writes, are “the mistake that made machine learning.” Notably, he argues, instead of creating a replicability crisis, they drove legitimate progress anyway — “mostly by sheer luck,” in his view. By understanding why, we can explain how benchmarks have since lost this accidental credibility in the age of LLMs, and how they might regain it. Quanta spoke to Hardt about what went wrong, and right, with benchmarks, and where to take them next. The interview has been condensed and edited for clarity. Hardt is fascinated by how benchmarks paradoxically helped start both a 25-year AI winter in the late 1980s and a deep learning revolution in the 2010s. Jerrit Peinelt for Quanta Magazine Let’s get the basics straight: What even is a benchmark? The recipe is simple. To evaluate a machine learning model, you take your data and split it into a training set and a test set. You let the model builders do whatever they want on the training set: Anything goes, no rules. But you use the test set only to compare and rank models — to have a leaderboard say, “This is currently state-of-the-art, this is number one, this is number two.” So a benchmark for a large language model today, like GPT-6 Astra or Claude Fable, might test an ability to solve difficult math problems or find security bugs in software . Right. The first benchmark, in fact, was created in 1959. It was a set of digits and letters printed on punch cards, meant to test how well different scanners could recognize written characters . Somebody introduced the train-test split and started a leaderboard. It wasn’t like there was some master plan. But that’s what we now call benchmarking, and it’s been the engine of progress in AI for about 60 years or so. What are benchmarks supposed to tell us? Traditionally, a benchmark is supposed to be like a thermometer. People train a model to do something, and then you come up with some kind of measurement procedure to see how good the model is. But in practice, benchmarking is more like a sports competition or a market. Benchmarks define the rules of the game, and people actively compete over them, and we let the best model win. Hardt cautions that the scores AI models receive on benchmarks don’t mean much. But comparisons, or rankings, among models do. Jerrit Peinelt for Quanta Magazine Can’t they be both? What’s the problem? Any machine learning textbook will tell you about the “holdout method” — that you should lock away the test set, and only use it once to rank the models. If you ignore this, you’re on thin ice. You might get very misleading results because you’re evaluating models that in some sense have knowledge of the test set. The fascinating thing is that machine learning as a discipline just ignored the warning. It took all these test sets and put them on the internet for everyone to use. It’s easy to put these test sets in a model’s development loop and to keep iterating on them. Is that what’s “broken” about benchmarks? If you look at a model’s accuracy numbers on one benchmark, and then you change the test set only slightly, you get completely different accuracy numbers. That’s the sense in which the benchmark is not working. If you have 90% accuracy on one dataset and 73% on another, which is it? I have no idea how good this model is. In areas such as loan screening, fraud detection, payment risk management, and AI-driven automated trading, model predictions directly impact the movement of funds and the approval of transactions. In such systems, not only model accuracy but also data reliability, response speed, handling of anomalies, and the traceability of decision-making become critical. Even if AUC or KS statistics improve during the research phase, that alone does not guarantee stability in actual business operations. In production environments, issues that were not fully replicated during model training occur, such as data arrival delays, external service outages, changes in feature definitions, and delays in confirming ground-truth labels. When considering production-level machine learning, it is necessary to view the predictive model not as an isolated algorithm, but as a single system that encompasses everything from data processing to final business decisions. Point-in-Time Data Integrity and Feature Consistency Machine learning systems at financial institutions utilize a variety of data sources. Loan screening uses repayment history, credit information, application data, and customer transaction behavior. Fraud detection analyzes payment history, device information, access patterns, transaction networks, and external risk information. These data sources have different update frequencies and processing latencies. In research environments, historical transaction data is often organized and missing information is imputed. However, in production, only the information available up to the actual moment of decision-making can be used. This is where Point-in-Time Correctness becomes critical. For example, consider using the number of transactions in the past 24 hours as a feature. Suppose that while training was based on the time the transaction actually occurred, the production environment aggregates data based on the time it was recorded in the database. If there is a delay in data arrival, the calculation results may differ even under the same 24-hour condition. Even if the model itself is functioning normally, the meaning of the input features changes. This is an example of Train-Serve Skew. To prevent this issue, it is necessary to consistently manage feature definitions, aggregation periods, missing value handling, data acquisition times, and version control. Implementing a Feature Store is an effective measure, but simply introducing one does not guarantee data accuracy. If incorrect time information is stored, there is a possibility that the same error will be reused throughout the organization. What is important is that each feature has the same meaning under the same conditions in both the research environment and the production environment. This challenge is also common in AI-driven quantitative trading. In the research and development of multi-factor market analysis and automated trading that KAEL AI works on, market prices, order book information, execution data, and derived indicators are updated at different frequencies. To correctly evaluate trading signals discovered from historical data, it is necessary to verify them using only the information that was actually available at that time. Data point-in-time consistency is a fundamental requirement for connecting financial machine learning research results to actual decision-making. Data drift does not necessarily mean model degradation In financial risk models, the Population Stability Index (PSI) is sometimes used to monitor changes in the distribution of features and prediction scores. In practice, there is a school of thought that caution is required when the PSI exceeds 0.1, and that it is considered a relatively large change when it exceeds 0.25. However, these are empirical guidelines and are not statistical standards that can be applied to all data and models. The results of PSI vary depending on the setting of split intervals, sample size, the distribution being compared, and the nature of the features. For example, in payment data with strong seasonality, a large difference in distribution can occur even if user behavior has changed normally. On the other hand, even if the distribution of features has hardly changed, if the relationship between those features and fraudulent transactions or defaults changes, the predictive power of the model may decline. Therefore, it is necessary to distinguish at least the following three things. The first is data quality issues. This includes an increase in missing values, changes in collection processing, and failures in acquiring external data. The second is changes in the target population. This is when customer composition, transaction channels, or usage behavior changes. The third is changes in predictive relationships. This is when the relationship between previously effective features and the prediction target changes. You should not take the same approach to these problems. If it is a data quality issue, you must first correct the data processing. If it is a change in customer composition, analysis by segment is necessary. If the predictive relationship itself is changing, re-evaluation or retraining of the model is considered. News.title: Meta Challenges China With New Open-Weight AI Model
News.description: Meta has announced a new open-weight model, Muse Spark Open, in a market that has historically been Chinese-dominated.
News.article_text: Meta has announced a new open-weight model, Muse Spark Open, in a market that has historically been Chinese-dominated. Key Takeaways Meta has released a new open-weight AI model called Muse Spark Open The release could potentially challenge Chinese dominance in the open-weight market Because of the added security advantages of open-weight models, businesses could increasingly turn to them as their performance starts to match up to closed models Meta has released Muse Spark Open, an open-weight AI model that could challenge frontrunners and boost Meta’s AI position. China currently dominates the open-weight market, with models such as Kimi K3 and GLM 5.5 among the most popular. However, Meta’s new model could give the West a significant leg-up. Open-weight models are cheaper and can be run locally, which brings serious security benefits. As AI becomes more of a security concern , the models winning in the open-weight category could prove deciders in the wider AI race. Meta Releases Muse Spark Open AI Model with Apple Meta has turned its attention to open-weight AI models with the release of Muse Spark Open, in a collaboration with Apple that sees the model able to run locally on Mac Studios. Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief of AI, said in a post on X that the new model is “the most capable US open-weight model to date.” Evaluation results released by the company on Thursday do suggest the model offers superior performance. This just in! View the top business tech deals for 2026 👨‍💻 See the list ⚡ According to Artificial Analysis’s Intelligence Index, Muse Spark Open sits ahead of several Western open-weight models, achieving a score of 39. Similarly, Spark Open either matches or tops rivals on multimodal and knowledge tasks. West Offered Boost in China AI Race Artificial Analysis’s Intelligence Index might have placed Muse Spark Open above some Western models, but it remains behind Z.ai’s GLM 5.5 and Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 , both of which are Chinese-owned. Z.ai and Moonshot AI, as well as DeepSeek, have been leading the charge when it comes to open-weight models. Mostly, they’ve been able to stay competitive with frontier labs by offering lower prices and maintaining solid performance metrics. While Western models from OpenAI and Anthropic generally perform better than Chinese models, it’s widely believed the gap is closing. The concern is so great for the US government that it has discouraged US businesses from using Chinese AI in the past. With the arrival of Muse Spark Open, however, the US might have a way to challenge Chinese open-weight authority . The new model’s release might also re-establish Meta in the US AI race, which has been dominated by the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI. Days before Spark Open was announced, Meta introduced Muse Wonder , which it said rivals the most advanced version of ChatGPT and Claude. Indeed, Artificial Analysis’s Intelligence Index placed Muse Wonder ahead of OpenAI’s GPT-Astra, Claude’s Fable 5, and Google’s Gemini 4. How Open-Weight Models Could Define the AI Race There are three types of AI models: closed, open-weight, and open-source. Of the three, open-source provides the most transparency, by allowing comprehensive access to their components and even allowing users to retrain models. Open-weight models let developers download their weights, or their parameters, and modify them. They don’t allow for the same accessibility as open-source models , but they offer more than closed models, which aren’t downloadable and keep much of their architecture hidden. Closed models make up today’s highest performing AI models . Think Claude Opus 5.5 or GPT-6. However, open-weight models are becoming increasingly popular for today’s businesses, due to clear advantages. The first advantage is price. Open-weight models are generally cheaper , with lower token costs, because they’re run by multiple hosts rather than by a single provider. Furthermore, open-weight models are stored locally on proprietary infrastructure, so data never leaves a company’s servers. This provides a security and privacy advantage , particularly for those working in industries that require confidential or sensitive customer data. Given the current climate of AI data breaches and cyber attacks, this is a big plus. As the security concerns around AI become more significant, businesses may increasingly turn to open-weight models to better protect themselves and their data. This could lead to open-weight models becoming the preference over closed models. It’s important to note that closed models do currently hold the edge when it comes to performance, especially around complex, multi-step reasoning. But, this gap could certainly change, and the US staking a claim in this currently Chinese-dominated market isn’t a bad idea. Webpage.body: Grounding AI agents in biological reality: Building blocks for autonomous wet labs October 16, 2026 Pooja Rao, Research Scientist, Petar Sirkovic, Software Engineer, and Annalisa Pawlosky, Research Scientist, Google We are bringing AI agents to the wet-lab bench at Google Research to navigate complex biological landscapes. By grounding agents in physical lab robotics, we can run fast closed-loop molecular design cycles where agents learn how to learn, ultimately discovering single-digit nanomolar protein binders for cancer targets. Quick links VERID paper Agentic aptamer sandbox paper Epitope excision paper × Frontier AI systems have the potential to transform biology research and drug discovery by intelligently navigating vast combinatorial search spaces (e.g., a single 100-amino-acid protein spans at least 20 100 possible sequences) calling for dynamic multi-candidate exploration. Our long-term research vision is that AI agents will not only ideate and analyze, but also run lab experiments to test their hypotheses, learn from the results, and self-improve to solve complex problems — all driven by human scientific agency. Realizing this vision requires solving two intertwined challenges: First, frontier models still do not reason reliably about 3-dimensional geometry and physical state — which poses a problem in the automation of the specialized liquid-handling robots that move reagents, track volumes, and execute molecular biology protocols in a wet lab. Second, while agentic hypothesis generation and in-silico design are advancing rapidly, needing repeated cycles of real-world feedback to validate the proposals and navigate vast search spaces, real-world wet-lab experiments have not kept pace, making experimental readouts more of a bottleneck than ever. In this post we share three research projects highlighting our progress on bridging the gap between in-silico AI exploration and real-world wet-lab experimentation: Enabling AI agents to perform safe, resource efficient experimentation grounded in physical measurements by using the VERID framework. Demonstrating closed-loop agentic scientific discoveries on our prototypes for aptamer and de-novo protein design. Grounding agents in physical reality First, we present the VERified Infrastructure for Discovery Laboratories (VERID) framework to bridge the gap between the high-level reasoning of AI agents and the complex, error-prone physical reality of a wet lab. It is a semantic digital twin of the laboratory workcell, i.e., a live, stateful 3D volumetric entity tree that tracks everything from robotic arm geometry to individual well volumes, reagent identities, and pipette tip inventory. The safety of a command depends on the live physical context as well as the code. An agent can generate syntactically valid code that is physically impossible (e.g., lowering an 8-channel pipette into a narrow trough that is too short), logistically invalid (e.g., aspirating from a depleted well), or scientifically compromised by unmodeled fluidic effects. play looping video pause looping video unmute video mute video Through VERID, an AI agent plans, simulates, and executes liquid-handling protocols on a liquid handling robot, combining synchronized multi-camera views with live state tracking to refine experiments across cycles. Built on top of the open-source PyLabRobot framework , VERID provides four core capabilities: Live 3D state tracking: Allow agents to check deck layout, well volumes, and available tips before acting. Fast virtual dry runs: Simulate protocols in seconds to catch collisions or empty wells before touching reagents. Hardware safety checks: Block invalid commands before they reach the robot. Synchronized video and action logs: Capture a complete record of every run for research rigor, reproducibility, and debugging. In our report , we show these capabilities in action through case studies. First, synchronized video and execution traces caught uneven dye stratification caused by dispensing too close to the well floor, allowing the agent to refine its mixing strategy. In the same campaign, the persistent digital twin state allowed the agent to recover mid-run from a plate-reader failure without re-pipetting. Second, when the simulator rejected an 8-channel aspiration that physically wouldn't fit in a narrow trough, the agent replanned on the fly and designed a targeted factorial diagnostic isolating a subtle bias caused by residual tip-wall carryover that replication alone would have missed. Finally, in a closed-loop self-play campaign, an agent iteratively designed and ran robot experiments to reconstruct blinded dye mixtures from overhead camera images, identifying its own optical and fluidic artifacts across runs to improve accuracy more than fivefold. Reproducible execution and full trace logs — capturing procedural variables like dwell times, evaporation, and plate layout — lay the groundwork for agents to eventually be able to separate biological signals from experimental noise as they explore and refine many candidates in parallel across rounds. Learning to learn with aptamers Agents need real experimental readouts to refine their hypotheses as computational models do not capture the full picture of what happens in a wet-lab reaction and cannot replace empirical validation. In “ Aptamers as a sandbox for lab-in-the-loop agentic molecular discovery ”, we use protein-binding DNA aptamers to prototype the lab in a closed loop with AI agents over 3 design-test-iteration cycles. Aptamer discovery is a type of experiment common in research efforts for clinical biomarker discovery. A complete aptamer design-test-analyze cycle takes just 7–10 days, as DNA can be chemically synthesized in pooled libraries and read out directly by sequencing.
